newsitem.title: PERU: Peru guerrillas release seven, still hold 74.
newsitem.headline: Peru guerrillas release seven, still hold 74.

text.p: Peruvian Marxist guerrillas freed on Wednesday seven more hostages, including four Japanese businessmen, leaving 74 more captives inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
The Red Cross identified the Japanese businessmen as Makoto Sekiguchi and Haruo Takahashi, from the Mitsui company, and Yonezo Urata and Toyoaki Toda, of Matsushita Electric.

Two Peruvians of Japanese descent -- Jose Kamiya, of the Sistemas Sukiyaki company, and Alberto Yamamoto, president of the government's national development institute (INADE) -- were also among the released captives.
The seventh released hostage was identified as Peruvian privatisation official Juan Assereto Duaret.

The seven men, all wearing jackets and looking in good health, walked out of the building with chief Red Cross representative Michel Minnig and Peruvian Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani who has acted as an observer in talks to end the crisis.
The freed men were immediately taken by bus to a police hospital for a routine medical checkup.
Wednesday's releases came 15 days after Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed a lavish reception at the residence on Dec. 17, originally taking more than 500 captives.

The remaining captives include President Alberto Fujimori's brother Pedro, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, a host of top Peruvian government and security force officials and a group of Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
Cipriani, a close ally of Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, welcomed the releases.
"I want to give thanks to God that on this day which the Church celebrates as the universal day of peace, we can see these brothers of ours in freedom," he told reporters outside the residence.
